title: The Compassion of the Word
english: Regarding the resurrection of the subject, it was already the fourth day of faith, and this was being held. But such a belief was not held strongly; for a little later it appears that he was still being spoken of as a certain wonderful man and one very able through virtue, but the perfect knowledge concerning him as the Divine Word was not yet learned, but was entirely unknown.

This is, being moved in spirit and by the Spirit usefully, he stirred himself up, like a brave champion seeing the enemies, and prepared himself against the opponents (John 11:33). He does not repeat the likeness toward men, nor does he demonstrate everywhere that which is above man, but he showed the most philanthropic compassion toward those mourning by the tear (John 11:35). This tear of the Lord is a provision of life for men. This mercy of the Savior overcomes those who are mourning. For this reason the Word descended into a body, so that he might cause those mourning to weep, and that the incorruptible divinity might be brought back toward the life-giving of men. “For we have a high priest able to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

The Lord offers indeed the priestly [office] and prayers on behalf of men, but the Son has a connection and harmony toward the Father regarding his purposes for men, and thus the goodwill of God toward men came to be, after the Christ's sympathy toward fellow-born men had occurred (John 11:41-42). He calls the following of the Father's purpose toward his own [purpose] the obedience of a father regarding the life of Lazarus, and he gives thanks concerning this.

And he demonstrates such sharpness of the Father's agreement toward his petition, so that even before asking and before uttering the word of my prayer, 'you have heard me,' he says (John 11:41-42), and not as something wonderful or paradoxical for a son to hear a father, nor as if they were separate and becoming something else; for 'I knew,' he says, 'that you always hear me'; for nothing divided what was between, nor are the purposes separated, but whatever is the will of the Son, this is driven from the Father, and the Father's unutterable will is with the Son.

Why then do you say that I have made the Eucharist, which it was fitting to make, since he is more benefited by the extraordinary and rather by goodness? (John 11:43-44). The calling of the one lying there by name was a symbol of friendship; for he called the youth, whom he raised, 'young man,' saying, 'Young man, I say to you, arise' (John 11:43), and the girl likewise 'Talitha koum', but he calls the friend and the familiar one by a more friendly name from the name itself, so that it might be a sign of the resurrection of those called friends by the Lord, whom the apostle says are dead in the Lord, and who will be called to meet him. This is consistent with what he said himself, that 'the dead shall come forth at the voice' (John 12:3) having heard 'the Son of God'.

And this exit from the tomb is more fearsome than the wonder according to the resurrection. Uncontradictedly, he also presented to the ignorant the authority of the Benefactor; for he did not go out walking many [people]; for he took away the authority of movement as if to show no suspicion of the ignorant, overturning their sophisms. Because of this, he also allows them to loose the risen one from the dead, so that they, having surrounded the bonds with their own hands and having freed him from the care, may stand as witnesses of the event to those who are absent. Why then does he pray, or rather take the form of a prayer? It is so that we may not think him to be contrary [to God]. And 'loose him and let him go', so that being led, he might not be praised with boasting (John 11:51).

It was not spoken by Caiaphas as a prophecy of the Spirit; for the prophetic Spirit did not devise a plot against Christ, but by some coincidence with the truth and the happening thing, he was granted the opportunity to sense such a thought, because he was high priest, so that he might foretell through his mouth the thing hidden from men until then and unknown. Mary fulfills a type of the Church, the Church of those from the Gentiles being set free from demons as 'seven demons had gone out' from this one, offering the fragrance of faith to the death of Christ and receiving from Christ power for her own head through the zeal and healing love concerning him, filling the whole world with the fragrance, as Paul says: 'we are the fragrance of Christ to God' (2 Cor 2:15).
Making the pity of the penitents a pretext for his own greed, he did not even receive this ministry as more faithful than the others, but...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Lowly Entry and Prophetic Symbolism
english: It is something lesser; for the service regarding material things is lesser than the service in the Word, just as the twelve also showed in the deeds of the apostles (John 12:13, 15). They were guarding the entrance of Phoenix and shouting welcome to the coming King of Israel, which is to say, they were bringing in Christ, the promised one, with a conspicuous honor into the city. And he, having received such honor from the people, is shaped into the most moderate state, fulfilling at once also the symbol foretold according to the prophecy.

And thus the seat upon the donkey has a moderate and humble character, having hidden within it the symbol of the not-so-pure people of that time who are to receive the coming of the Lord. But a donkey is not clean according to the law. And the prophet Zechariah cried out, evangelizing Zion indeed, freeing the King of all from fears and redeeming her from mighty enemies, but by the symbol showing him being led by the nations and used by a new people, since even he was a colt, upon which he comes sitting.

Therefore, necessarily also in rank, the Lord performed the miracle concerning Lazarus (John 12:17, 19), so that having this happened, he might be honored conspicuously by the multitude, and because of this honor, the Pharisees, having suffered greatly, might counsel against him, and thus the passion might be fulfilled, which indeed happens (John 12:19). They see, therefore, that they argue in vain against the faith toward Christ, they separate the believers in vain, they turn away the rest in vain, some by arguing, others even by threatening. All things, therefore, they say, are useless, if they turn toward his undoing.

He shows the honor descending from above from the Father toward his own human part which is below and is clearly seen and leads men toward life eternal and immortal (John 12:25, 26), not presenting to us the gift of life coming in any other way, or through him insofar as he is a heavenly power, since he himself also foretold that he would give eternal life to those who follow him by stepping, which bound him to say as the life springs forth. Here much of the human is shown, also showing a nature not willing to die, that he was not outside of human sufferings (John 12:27, 28).

For lest some might say that he easily disregards death, he shows by being outside of danger that he spoke these things in a way appropriate to the situation, as a man being troubled and seeking deliverance, if it were not useful. What he says is such: 'Even if I am now troubled, having known death, I do not say so as to flee from it; for it is necessary to bear the burden; for I do not say, deliver me from this hour, but, glorify your name, that is, lead now to the cross' (John 12:28). These things he says, introducing us into a pattern of manliness.

There is no dialogue in a voice from the Father to the Son, for the divine is beyond voice; rather, a sound is sent from heaven to the ears of men from the face of the Father toward the Son, so that those hearing might more greatly remember Christ and know his divinity which is above man. Nor is glory attributed to the Father as always having it, except insofar as it shines forth and is known for the recognition of men; nor is the Son to be considered as being glorified from a lack of glory, except insofar as he, formerly unseen according to the flesh, is made manifest in the eyes of men.

The voice did not take the ears of those present, but the fact that it happened is what is glorified; for it was a doctrine among them from the fathers that audible voices are not to be received from the mouth of God, since even Moses and all the rest, whoever had spoken concerning the word of God having been heard, signaled to men that the manner of the conversation was that of an angel, saying. If indeed we also shall set the one who brought the voice to be an angel, it is well regarding the human face to have heard the paternal voice from above through an angel. Jesus answered and said: 'This voice did not happen through me' (John 12:30); for even he who knew the Father and the things of the Father was not seen.

Therefore, does he allow one to think anything small about him, or even as about a prophet, to know who he is before God? See, lest 'glorify your name' be the same as being referred to the Savior who exists as the Word of God. So also is the name of the Father, but a name not that which is composed of syllables nor signified in sounds, but that which makes manifest the identity of the Father. According to this is the understanding of the name of God and that which is said in the Psalm: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' (Psalm 22:22); for how else is a declaration of the name [understanding] of God?
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Ignorance of the Prophets and the Nature of Faith
english: They are shown to be ignorant regarding the prophets and lacking precise knowledge of the written things; for they have received voices saying that the Christ remains forever, but they did not understand the mystery of death occurring in between and the brief dissolution of the soul from the body (John 12:36).

He does not wish to be seized while wandering in the midst or discussing in between, but withdrawing and overshadowing himself; for in this He reproved the treachery of the traitor as a hired teacher receiving wages, and He guarded His own gentleness and was completely removed from audacity, even to the point of coming into the midst only to testify the truth; for it was not an act of wrath against the Savior that their work had to be, but a plan of malice; for everything done out of wrath is lesser for condemnation, but the extreme is to do evil with a plan.

Let us not think that a hardening and a callousness of heart is brought on by God as the operation of the holy power (John 12:40), but rather a concession to the divine judgment, and the operation of the evil and opposing power.

It is evident that before the fully revealed departure these things were said to the Lord (John 12:44-45), and after these words He withdrew, whom John, repeating, foretells having seen both the believers and those guarding their confession. He reproved the terrible sin of standing against confession; for he said that those doing this are setting aside faith in God; for one does not believe in something other than God, who is seen in Him, because, he says, the Father is seen in the Son. Therefore, just as one who received him as a servant did not receive the one who sent him, so he spoke of the one believing in Him as believing in God; for he would no longer follow as the one seeing Me sees the one who sent Me; for the faith toward the one serving is directed toward the servant seeing the sender, but he who, in the vision of the Son, sees the Father, does not turn beyond Jesus to the Father, but remaining in the Son and standing, receives the Father.

So that the one believing in me does not believe in me until he has the manifestation of the flesh and the human face. From the time that he who leads forward and brings up the hearts of men sees me, he says, he sees me fivefold; that is, the one able to know through insight who is present through the flesh, and grasping with a beautiful theory, this one finds me truly, and he finds in his faith toward me the faith toward the Father. So then, as he was saying, the one believing in me does not believe in a mere human, but in the power of God, in whom the Father is known and believed.

His words are spoken with authority, because he is both Creator and the lawgiver to his own creatures, according to the word of God, through whom all things came into being (John 1:3), who came to his own (John 1:11) and converses with authority, not as if he were any servant of the words given from God. For to none of such things would the 'I say to you' and the comparison to the laws toward the gods be appropriate; for having placed alongside what was spoken from a divine person the 'you shall not murder' and the 'you shall not commit adultery,' he brings forth for each case the 'but I say to you.' Nor is the lawgiving foreign to the Savior, nor does he speak from revelation, nor does he converse as if things were commanded, if we think according to divinity his own nature and his eternal existence.
First and readily available is the benefit of humility exceeding all by example and of the greatest love. He speaks of a transition from human weakness to the super-heavenly glory.

The washing of the feet here alludes to the deeper matter, which seems to be a preparation of the apostolic feet for the work of the apostolate; for he sends them having been cleansed with the feet, through the purity being given by himself, so that indeed they might be able to run through the world, promising the gospels of salvation, according to the saying, 'how beautiful are the feet of those announcing peace' (Romans 10:15). Since they were clean, he said, it remains for the body also to have the cleansing of the feet; that is, so that they might not only be clean for themselves, but also in the course of their journey might be clean, bringing purity to all men. And he said that they are not all clean because of the twelfth one in them having all the uncleanness in himself.
